title: Respiratory Pharmacology
summary: Bronchodilators, inhaled steroids and biologics for asthma and COPD.

lessons.title: Airway Physiology

levels.kid: When you breathe in, air travels down a tube in your neck that splits into smaller and smaller tubes, like the branches of an upside-down tree. At the tips are tiny balloons where oxygen jumps into your blood. The tubes have little muscles wrapped around them. In asthma, those muscles squeeze too tight, the inside gets swollen, and sticky mucus clogs things up. Breathing becomes like sucking air through a skinny straw, and you might hear a whistle called wheezing. Asthma medicines either relax the squeezing muscles or calm the swelling so the tubes stay open.
levels.hs:
The airways branch from the **trachea** into **bronchi**, then smaller **bronchioles**, ending in **alveoli** where gas exchange happens. Bronchi and bronchioles are wrapped in **smooth muscle**.

**Nerve control of airway muscle:**
- **Parasympathetic** nerves (vagus) release **acetylcholine**, which acts on M3 receptors and **narrows** the airways (bronchoconstriction) and increases mucus.
- Airway muscle has **beta-2 receptors**. Adrenaline in the blood activates them and **opens** the airways (bronchodilation). There are few direct sympathetic nerves to the muscle.

**Asthma** is a chronic inflammatory disease: the airways are hyperresponsive, so triggers (allergens, exercise, cold air, viruses, smoke) cause reversible narrowing. Inflammation involves eosinophils, mast cells and Th2 immune signals.

**COPD** (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), usually from smoking, causes airflow limitation that is not fully reversible, with neutrophilic inflammation, airway damage and alveolar destruction (emphysema).

**Measuring airflow:** spirometry measures **FEV1** (air blown out in one second) and **FVC**. A low FEV1/FVC ratio means obstruction. In asthma, FEV1 improves a lot after a bronchodilator.

**Two big drug strategies:** relax the muscle (bronchodilators) and treat the inflammation (anti-inflammatories).
levels.college:
**Smooth muscle signaling.** Contraction depends on intracellular Ca²⁺ and myosin light chain phosphorylation. M3 receptors (Gq) activate PLC, IP3-mediated Ca²⁺ release and RhoA/Rho kinase, which inhibits myosin light chain phosphatase (calcium sensitization). β2 receptors (Gs) raise cAMP and activate PKA, which lowers Ca²⁺, phosphorylates myosin light chain kinase to reduce its activity, and opens large-conductance Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channels, causing relaxation. Phosphodiesterases (PDE3, PDE4) break down cAMP. Presynaptic M2 autoreceptors limit acetylcholine release; their dysfunction in viral infection and asthma increases vagal bronchoconstriction.

**Inflammatory pathways in asthma.** Type 2 (T2-high) inflammation: allergens and epithelial damage release alarmins (TSLP, IL-33, IL-25), activating Th2 cells and group 2 innate lymphoid cells to produce IL-4 (IgE class switching), IL-5 (eosinophil growth and survival) and IL-13 (mucus, hyperresponsiveness, FeNO via iNOS). IgE on mast cells triggers release of histamine, leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4) and prostaglandin D2 on allergen exposure. Biomarkers: blood eosinophils, FeNO, total and specific IgE. T2-low asthma involves neutrophils or few inflammatory cells and responds less to steroids.

**COPD.** Cigarette smoke activates macrophages and epithelium, recruiting neutrophils and CD8⁺ T cells; proteases (neutrophil elastase, MMP-12) destroy alveolar walls. Oxidative stress reduces histone deacetylase 2 (HDAC2) activity, which explains relative steroid resistance. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early panacinar emphysema.

**Drug delivery.** Inhaled therapy delivers drug to the lung with low systemic exposure. Particle size matters: particles of roughly 1 to 5 micrometers reach the lower airways. Most of an inhaled dose is swallowed and absorbed orally, so oral bioavailability and first-pass metabolism determine systemic side effects. Technique (metered-dose inhaler with spacer, dry powder inhaler needing fast inspiration) is a major cause of treatment failure.
levels.phd:
**Airway hyperresponsiveness beyond inflammation.** Hyperresponsiveness persists in some patients despite suppressed inflammation, implicating structural remodeling: smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, subepithelial fibrosis, goblet cell metaplasia and angiogenesis. Bronchial thermoplasty, which reduces smooth muscle mass with radiofrequency energy, was developed on this rationale. Mechanical factors also matter: deep inspirations normally stretch smooth muscle and reduce actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling, and loss of this bronchoprotective effect is characteristic of asthma.

**β2 receptor regulation.** Chronic agonist exposure leads to GRK phosphorylation, β-arrestin binding, internalization and downregulation, contributing to tolerance to bronchoprotection. Glucocorticoids increase β2 receptor transcription, while β2 agonists (via PKA and CREB) can enhance glucocorticoid receptor nuclear translocation, the molecular basis for synergy in combination inhalers. The Arg16Gly polymorphism of ADRB2 was linked to reduced response to regular agonist use in some studies, but genotype-guided therapy did not prove useful in practice.

**Epithelial barrier and alarmins.** The epithelium is now viewed as the conductor of asthma: viral injury, pollutants and proteases (from house dust mite allergens such as Der p 1, which cleaves tight junctions) trigger TSLP and IL-33 release upstream of both T2 and non-T2 pathways. Tezepelumab, an anti-TSLP antibody, reduces exacerbations across eosinophil levels, supporting this upstream model.

**Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.** Hyperventilation of dry air causes airway surface dehydration and hyperosmolarity, triggering mast cell mediator release (leukotrienes, PGD2). This explains why pretreatment with SABA or leukotriene antagonists helps, and why warm humid air protects.

**Heterogeneity.** Cluster analyses (for example from the Severe Asthma Research Program) define phenotypes such as early-onset allergic, late-onset eosinophilic and obesity-associated asthma, guiding precision therapy.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis before drugs.** Confirm variable airflow obstruction with spirometry and bronchodilator reversibility, peak flow variability or a challenge test when spirometry is normal. Many patients labeled asthmatic have something else: vocal cord dysfunction (inducible laryngeal obstruction), heart failure, dysfunctional breathing or COPD. Measure biomarkers (blood eosinophils, FeNO, IgE) to phenotype the disease, ideally before steroids lower them.

**Assessment of severity and control.** Ask about night symptoms, reliever use, activity limitation and exacerbations needing oral steroids or emergency care. Poor control usually reflects poor inhaler technique, poor adherence, smoking, ongoing allergen or occupational exposure, or comorbidities (rhinosinusitis, reflux, obesity, anxiety). Check these before adding drugs.

**Acute asthma red flags:** inability to speak in sentences, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, rising or normal CO₂ in a breathless patient (a sign of fatigue), and altered mental status. These signal life-threatening asthma requiring ICU-level care.

**Neuro and neurosurgical relevance.**
- Beta-blockers, including eye drops, can trigger severe bronchospasm in asthma; this matters with perioperative blood pressure control.
- Aspirin and other COX-1 inhibitors cause bronchospasm in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (with nasal polyps), relevant to postoperative pain plans.
- High spinal cord injury weakens breathing muscles and the cough, while unopposed vagal tone can cause bronchospasm and secretions.
- Neuromuscular diseases (myasthenia, ALS, Guillain-Barré) cause restrictive patterns, not obstruction; spirometry helps distinguish them.
- Inhaled anesthetics (sevoflurane) are bronchodilators; airway instrumentation can trigger bronchospasm in poorly controlled asthma, so control is optimized before elective surgery.

keyPoints: M3 (Gq) muscarinic signaling constricts airways; β2 (Gs, cAMP) relaxes them
Asthma: reversible, hyperresponsive, often T2 eosinophilic inflammation
COPD: incompletely reversible obstruction, neutrophilic, relative steroid resistance
T2 cytokines: IL-4 (IgE), IL-5 (eosinophils), IL-13 (mucus, FeNO); alarmins TSLP/IL-33
Low FEV1/FVC means obstruction; reversibility suggests asthma
Inhaler technique and adherence are the most common causes of poor control

lessons.title: Beta-2 Agonists and Antimuscarinics

levels.kid: Imagine the muscles around your breathing tubes are like a fist squeezing a garden hose. Two kinds of medicines help the fist let go. The first kind presses a "relax" button on the muscle. A fast one works in minutes, so it's the rescue puffer people carry for an asthma attack. Slower ones last all day or all night. The second kind blocks a "squeeze" message the nerves send. Both kinds are breathed in, so they go straight to the lungs where they are needed. They can make your hands a bit shaky or your heart beat faster for a little while.
levels.hs:
**Bronchodilators** open the airways by relaxing airway smooth muscle.

**Beta-2 agonists** activate β2 receptors:
- **SABA** (short-acting): **albuterol (salbutamol)**, levalbuterol. Work within minutes and last a few hours: the classic rescue inhaler.
- **LABA** (long-acting): **salmeterol**, **formoterol** (12 hours), and once-daily vilanterol, olodaterol, indacaterol. Formoterol starts working quickly, so it can also be a reliever.

**Antimuscarinics** block acetylcholine at M3 receptors:
- **SAMA**: **ipratropium**, used with albuterol in emergencies and in COPD.
- **LAMA**: **tiotropium**, umeclidinium, glycopyrronium, aclidinium. Once daily; a mainstay of COPD.

**Important rules:**
- In asthma, a **LABA must never be used alone**: always with an inhaled corticosteroid, because LABA alone was linked to asthma deaths.
- Using a SABA alone without an anti-inflammatory is no longer recommended for asthma; many guidelines now use an ICS-formoterol inhaler as the reliever.
- In COPD, LAMA and LABA are the main treatments.

**Side effects:** β2 agonists cause tremor, fast heart rate and low potassium; antimuscarinics cause dry mouth and, rarely, urinary retention or worsening of narrow-angle glaucoma.
levels.college:
**β2 agonist pharmacology.** Selectivity for β2 over β1 is relative; at high exposures, tachycardia arises from both β1 stimulation and reflex responses to β2-mediated vasodilation. β2 activation drives K⁺ into cells via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, causing hypokalemia (useful in treating hyperkalemia), and stimulates glycogenolysis and lactate production. Lactic acidosis can occur with intensive nebulized albuterol in acute asthma.

**Duration mechanisms.** Salmeterol's long lipophilic tail anchors in the membrane or an exosite near the receptor, allowing repeated engagement of the active site; its onset is slow and it is a partial agonist. Formoterol is moderately lipophilic, forming a membrane depot, with fast onset and full agonism. Ultra-long agents (indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol) support once-daily use.

**Safety history.** The SMART trial (salmeterol monotherapy) showed increased asthma-related deaths, especially in some subgroups, leading to boxed warnings. Large trials of LABA combined with ICS in one inhaler showed no excess serious events, and the warning on combination products was removed in 2017. A LABA without an ICS in asthma remains contraindicated.

**Antimuscarinics.** Ipratropium and tiotropium are quaternary ammonium compounds, poorly absorbed systemically and do not cross the blood-brain barrier. Tiotropium has kinetic selectivity: it dissociates slowly from M3 and M1 receptors but quickly from M2 autoreceptors, which favors bronchodilation over increased acetylcholine release. LAMAs reduce COPD exacerbations; tiotropium is also add-on therapy in severe asthma.

**Guideline shifts.** GINA (2019 onward) no longer recommends SABA-only treatment for adolescents and adults, because SABA overuse is linked to exacerbations and deaths; as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol reduces severe exacerbations. Maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) uses one ICS-formoterol inhaler for both. In COPD, LAMA-LABA dual therapy is standard for symptomatic patients, adding ICS mainly when eosinophils are raised and exacerbations are frequent.
levels.phd:
**Structural pharmacology of β2AR.** The β2 adrenergic receptor was the first hormone-activated GPCR crystallized (2007) and captured in complex with Gs (2011, Kobilka and colleagues; Nobel 2012 with Lefkowitz). Agonists engage serine residues on transmembrane helix 5 via catechol-like hydroxyls, triggering outward movement of TM6 to open the G protein binding site. Salmeterol's exosite binding was confirmed structurally, its aryloxyalkyl tail lying in an extracellular vestibule, explaining sustained activity with reduced efficacy.

**Biased signaling and tolerance.** Agonists differ in efficacy for Gs versus β-arrestin pathways. Regular SABA use causes tolerance to bronchoprotection (against challenges) more than to bronchodilation, partly via receptor desensitization and possibly increased airway responsiveness after withdrawal. Some researchers proposed that β-arrestin-mediated signaling contributes to airway inflammation, and that β2 inverse agonists might even reduce hyperresponsiveness in mice; this hypothesis remains experimental.

**Racemic albuterol.** (R)-albuterol is the active enantiomer; (S)-albuterol was hypothesized to increase hyperresponsiveness and is cleared more slowly, but levalbuterol showed no consistent clinical advantage, a cautionary example of chiral switching.

**Muscarinic receptor subtypes in the airway.** M1 receptors in parasympathetic ganglia facilitate transmission; M2 on postganglionic nerve terminals inhibit acetylcholine release; M3 on smooth muscle and glands drive contraction and secretion. Viral neuraminidase and eosinophil major basic protein impair M2 function, increasing vagal reflex bronchoconstriction, an explanation for virus-induced exacerbations. Acetylcholine also acts on non-neuronal targets (epithelium, inflammatory cells, fibroblasts), suggesting antimuscarinics have anti-remodeling effects beyond bronchodilation.

**Bifunctional molecules.** MABAs (muscarinic antagonist and β2 agonist in one molecule, for example batefenterol) were designed to deliver both mechanisms at fixed ratio; development has been limited.
levels.expert:
**Acute asthma in the emergency department.** Repeated or continuous nebulized SABA, ipratropium added in moderate to severe attacks, systemic corticosteroids early, oxygen to target saturation, and IV magnesium sulfate for severe cases. Monitor potassium and lactate with intensive β2 agonist use. Escalation for life-threatening features involves ICU teams.

**Chronic asthma.** Every patient needs an inhaled steroid-containing regimen. Teach the reliever plan clearly, check technique with each device, and review frequent reliever use as a marker of poor control. A patient filling many SABA canisters a year is at high risk of a severe attack.

**COPD.** Start a long-acting bronchodilator (LAMA or LAMA-LABA) for symptoms; add ICS mainly when blood eosinophils are high and exacerbations continue. Pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking cessation matter as much as inhalers.

**Pitfalls.**
- Nebulized ipratropium leaking around a mask can reach the eye and trigger acute angle-closure glaucoma, especially combined with albuterol; use a mouthpiece in at-risk patients.
- Antimuscarinics can cause urinary retention in older men with prostate enlargement.
- Tremor and palpitations are common; marked tachycardia or arrhythmia in older patients with heart disease warrants review.
- β2 agonists lower potassium; combined with diuretics, steroids and theophylline, hypokalemia can be significant.

**Neuro relevance.** Anisocoria after ipratropium nebulization (pharmacological mydriasis from aerosol in the eye) can mimic a third nerve palsy from herniation. Clues: the patient is alert and otherwise neurologically normal, and the dilated pupil does not constrict with pilocarpine. This is a classic trap for neurosurgical consults in the emergency department.

keyPoints: SABA (albuterol) is the classic reliever; LABA (salmeterol, formoterol) lasts 12-24 h
LABA monotherapy is contraindicated in asthma; always pair with ICS
GINA: ICS-formoterol is the preferred reliever; SABA-only is no longer advised
LAMAs (tiotropium) block M3 and are central in COPD
β2 agonist adverse effects: tremor, tachycardia, hypokalemia, lactic acidosis
Ipratropium in the eye causes a fixed dilated pupil that can mimic third nerve palsy

lessons.title: Inhaled Corticosteroids

levels.kid: In asthma, the inside of the breathing tubes is puffy and red, like a scraped knee that stays irritated. This makes the tubes extra sensitive, so they squeeze easily. Inhaled steroid medicines are like a calming cream for the inside of the lungs. You breathe them in every day, even when you feel fine, and over weeks the puffiness goes down, so attacks happen much less. They don't work fast like the rescue puffer. After using one, people rinse their mouth and spit, so a yeast germ doesn't grow there. This kind of steroid is a calming medicine that works like the body's own stress hormone.
levels.hs:
**Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)** are the most important **controller** medicines in asthma. Examples: **fluticasone, budesonide, beclomethasone, mometasone, ciclesonide**.

**What they do:** they reduce airway inflammation, the number of inflammatory cells (especially eosinophils), swelling and mucus, and they make airways less hyperresponsive. Over time they reduce symptoms, attacks, hospital visits and asthma deaths.

**How they work:** steroids enter cells and bind the **glucocorticoid receptor**. The complex moves to the nucleus and turns down genes for inflammatory signals (cytokines) and turns up anti-inflammatory genes.

**Using them well:**
- Use every day (or, in newer plans, combined with formoterol as needed), because benefit builds over days to weeks.
- They do not relieve an attack in minutes.
- Rinse the mouth and spit after use, and use a spacer with a metered-dose inhaler.

**Side effects:**
- Local: **oral thrush** (yeast infection), hoarse voice.
- Systemic effects are much smaller than with steroid pills, but at high exposures they can include slightly slower growth in children, bone thinning, cataracts and adrenal suppression.

In **COPD**, ICS help mainly patients with frequent flare-ups and high blood eosinophils, and they raise pneumonia risk.
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** Glucocorticoids bind the cytosolic glucocorticoid receptor (GRα), releasing chaperones (HSP90). The complex translocates to the nucleus and acts by:
- **Transrepression:** tethering to and inhibiting NF-κB and AP-1, and recruiting HDAC2 to deacetylate histones at inflammatory gene promoters, suppressing IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, GM-CSF, chemokines and iNOS.
- **Transactivation:** binding glucocorticoid response elements to induce anti-inflammatory proteins (MKP-1, GILZ, annexin A1/lipocortin, IκBα) and β2 receptors. Many metabolic side effects (gluconeogenesis) are also transactivation-driven.

Effects include eosinophil apoptosis, reduced mast cell numbers in the mucosa, lower FeNO and reduced plasma exudation. Benefit appears within days, with maximal effect on hyperresponsiveness over weeks to months.

**Pharmacokinetic design for the lung.** The ideal ICS has high receptor affinity, high lung retention and low systemic exposure:
- **High first-pass metabolism** of the swallowed fraction (fluticasone and mometasone have very low oral bioavailability).
- **High protein binding** and rapid systemic clearance.
- **Prodrugs** activated by lung esterases: beclomethasone dipropionate to the active monopropionate; ciclesonide to des-ciclesonide.
- **Lipophilicity and esterification:** budesonide forms reversible fatty acid esters in airway cells, prolonging retention.

The lung-deposited fraction is absorbed directly, bypassing first pass, so systemic exposure depends largely on lung delivery.

**Dose-response.** Most benefit is achieved at low to medium exposures; the curve is flat above that while systemic effects keep rising. Step-up therapy usually adds a LABA rather than increasing the steroid.

**Interactions.** Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, cobicistat, itraconazole) block fluticasone and budesonide metabolism, causing iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and adrenal suppression. Beclomethasone is preferred in these patients.
levels.phd:
**Steroid resistance.** Some patients with severe asthma and most with COPD respond poorly to steroids. Mechanisms include reduced HDAC2 activity from oxidative stress (tyrosine nitration and PI3Kδ activation), GR phosphorylation by p38 MAPK and other kinases that impairs nuclear translocation, increased expression of the dominant-negative GRβ isoform (induced by IL-17, IL-2 and IL-4 in some studies), and Th17 or neutrophilic inflammation, which is relatively insensitive to steroids (steroids actually prolong neutrophil survival). Low-dose theophylline restores HDAC2 activity in vitro, and macrolides and PI3Kδ inhibitors have been studied to reverse resistance.

**Dissociated GR agonists.** Efforts to separate transrepression (anti-inflammatory) from transactivation (metabolic side effects) led to selective GR agonists and modulators (SEGRAs, SEGRMs). The model proved too simple: some anti-inflammatory effects require transactivation (MKP-1, GILZ), and some side effects involve transrepression. Inhaled SEGRAs did not show clear advantages in trials.

**Growth in children.** The CAMP study found regular budesonide in childhood reduced final adult height by about a centimeter, mostly in the first years of treatment and without progression. This small, real effect is weighed against the benefits of controlling asthma, which itself affects growth.

**Pneumonia in COPD.** ICS raise pneumonia risk in COPD, with fluticasone showing a stronger signal than budesonide in observational studies, possibly related to its greater lipophilicity, longer airway residence and stronger local immunosuppression. Withdrawal studies (WISDOM) showed ICS can be removed safely from many patients with low eosinophils, while eosinophil counts above roughly 300 cells per microliter predict benefit.

**Bone and eye.** Long-term high exposure is associated with reduced bone mineral density, posterior subcapsular cataracts and glaucoma in susceptible people, relationships that show a dose-response in epidemiological data.
levels.expert:
**Starting and adjusting.** Every adolescent and adult with asthma should receive an ICS-containing treatment, either daily maintenance or as-needed ICS-formoterol for milder disease. Step up when control is poor after checking technique, adherence and triggers; step down after a few months of good control to the lowest effective level.

**Technique and practicalities.**
- Metered-dose inhalers: use a spacer, slow deep inhalation, breath-hold.
- Dry powder inhalers: fast, forceful inhalation; not suitable for young children or during severe attacks.
- Rinse and spit to reduce thrush and dysphonia.
- Count doses; empty inhalers that patients think are working are a common hidden failure.

**Adverse effect surveillance.** Monitor growth in children. At high exposures for prolonged periods, consider adrenal suppression, especially in children and in patients who also take nasal or skin steroids. Adrenal crisis has occurred in children on high-exposure fluticasone, presenting with hypoglycemia, seizures or collapse during illness or surgery.

**Drug interactions.** Ask about antiretrovirals boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat and strong azole antifungals. Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome followed by adrenal crisis on withdrawal is a well-described, preventable harm.

**Perioperative and neurosurgical points.**
- Patients on high-exposure ICS or recent oral steroids may need stress-dose steroid cover around major surgery.
- Poorly controlled asthma before elective surgery should be optimized, sometimes with a short oral steroid course.
- Neurosurgical patients often receive dexamethasone for brain tumor edema; in asthma patients, this improves asthma control temporarily, but hyperglycemia, infection risk and steroid myopathy (which weakens breathing muscles) matter.

**COPD.** Reserve ICS for patients with frequent exacerbations and eosinophilia, or asthma-COPD overlap; avoid ICS alone in COPD.

keyPoints: ICS are the cornerstone controller for asthma; benefit builds over days to weeks
GR complex suppresses NF-κB/AP-1 genes and recruits HDAC2
Low oral bioavailability and lung-activated prodrugs limit systemic exposure
Local adverse effects: thrush and dysphonia; rinse and spit
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir) with fluticasone cause Cushing syndrome
In COPD, ICS benefit is mainly in high eosinophils; they raise pneumonia risk

lessons.title: Leukotriene Modifiers and Methylxanthines

levels.kid: When allergies or asthma act up, some cells in your airways spill out tiny troublemaker chemicals called leukotrienes. They make the tubes squeeze, swell and get gooey. One kind of medicine is a pill that blocks the troublemakers from landing, like putting a lid on a trash can so the mess can't get out. Another old medicine is related to the caffeine in coffee and tea. It can help relax the breathing tubes, but too much of it makes the heart race and can be dangerous, so doctors check its level in the blood with a test.
levels.hs:
**Leukotrienes** are inflammatory chemicals made from **arachidonic acid** by the enzyme **5-lipoxygenase**. The cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) cause bronchoconstriction, mucus, swelling and attract eosinophils.

**Leukotriene modifiers:**
- **Montelukast** and zafirlukast block the CysLT1 receptor. Montelukast is a once-daily pill.
- **Zileuton** blocks 5-lipoxygenase, so leukotrienes are not made.

**Uses:** mild asthma (as an alternative to ICS, though less effective), add-on therapy, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, allergic rhinitis, and **aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease**.

**Warning:** montelukast carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects (sleep problems, vivid dreams, agitation, depression and suicidal thoughts), especially in young people. Families are told to watch for mood changes.

**Methylxanthines:** **theophylline** (and IV aminophylline) are related to caffeine. They relax airway muscle, but their benefit is modest and they have a **narrow therapeutic index**: levels just above the useful range cause nausea, fast heart rate, arrhythmias and seizures. Many drugs (like ciprofloxacin and erythromycin) raise theophylline levels; smoking lowers them. Blood levels are monitored.

**Roflumilast**, a PDE4 inhibitor pill, reduces flare-ups in severe COPD with chronic bronchitis.
levels.college:
**Leukotriene biosynthesis.** Cytosolic phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid; 5-lipoxygenase (5-LO), with 5-LO-activating protein (FLAP), forms LTA4. LTA4 hydrolase makes LTB4 (a neutrophil chemoattractant acting on BLT1), while LTC4 synthase conjugates glutathione to form LTC4, exported and converted to LTD4 and LTE4. CysLTs act on CysLT1 (bronchoconstriction, vascular leak, eosinophil recruitment) and CysLT2 receptors.

**Agents.**
- **Montelukast**: selective CysLT1 antagonist; well absorbed; CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 metabolism. Effects are additive with ICS but smaller.
- **Zafirlukast**: CYP2C9 inhibitor (raises warfarin effect); rare hepatotoxicity; must be taken away from food.
- **Zileuton**: 5-LO inhibitor, blocking both CysLTs and LTB4; requires liver enzyme monitoring; CYP1A2 inhibitor (raises theophylline).

**Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease** combines asthma, nasal polyps and respiratory reactions to COX-1 inhibitors. COX-1 inhibition removes PGE2's brake on 5-LO and mast cells, causing a surge in CysLTs. Leukotriene modifiers help; aspirin desensitization is an option.

**Theophylline.** Mechanisms: nonselective PDE inhibition (raising cAMP), adenosine receptor antagonism (responsible for many adverse effects, including seizures and arrhythmias), and HDAC2 activation at low concentrations. Clearance via CYP1A2 is reduced by fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, erythromycin, heart failure, liver disease and viral fever, and increased by smoking, rifampin, carbamazepine and phenytoin. Toxicity: vomiting, tachyarrhythmias, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, seizures (which can be refractory). Severe toxicity may need extracorporeal removal (hemodialysis); multiple-dose activated charcoal enhances elimination.

**Roflumilast.** Selective PDE4 inhibitor reducing neutrophilic inflammation; for severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and frequent exacerbations. Adverse effects: diarrhea, nausea, weight loss and psychiatric effects (insomnia, depression, suicidality).
levels.phd:
**Montelukast neuropsychiatric effects.** Postmarketing reports led to an FDA boxed warning in 2020. Mechanisms are uncertain: montelukast crosses the blood-brain barrier, CysLT1 receptors are found on neurons, microglia and the blood-brain barrier, and montelukast has off-target activity, including at GPR17 (a receptor in oligodendrocyte development). Ironically, the same CNS activity led to repurposing studies in neuroinflammation, stroke and neurodegeneration. Pharmacovigilance analyses support an association, especially with sleep disturbance in children, although confounding by asthma severity and psychiatric comorbidity is hard to exclude.

**Adenosine and seizures.** Endogenous adenosine is a powerful anticonvulsant acting through A1 receptors, and seizure termination depends partly on adenosine release. Theophylline antagonizes A1 receptors, explaining both its proconvulsant effect and why theophylline seizures can be prolonged and refractory, sometimes with poor outcomes. Caffeine shares this mechanism at much lower potency. In status epilepticus caused by theophylline, benzodiazepines and barbiturates are used, and phenytoin is considered less effective.

**Theophylline as an HDAC2 activator.** At concentrations below those needed for bronchodilation, theophylline increases HDAC2 activity by inhibiting PI3Kδ, potentially restoring steroid responsiveness in COPD. The TWICS trial of low-dose theophylline added to ICS in COPD found no reduction in exacerbations, an example of an attractive mechanism failing a pragmatic trial.

**PDE4 subtype pharmacology.** PDE4 has four genes (A to D). PDE4B mediates much of the anti-inflammatory effect, while PDE4D in the area postrema is linked to nausea and emesis, the dose-limiting effect of PDE4 inhibitors. Subtype-selective and inhaled PDE4 inhibitors, and the dual PDE3/4 inhibitor ensifentrine (inhaled, approved for COPD in 2024), aim to widen the therapeutic window.
levels.expert:
**Where these drugs fit.** Leukotriene receptor antagonists are add-on or alternative controllers, less effective than ICS. They are reasonable when patients cannot use inhalers, for concurrent allergic rhinitis, for exercise-induced symptoms, or in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Theophylline has largely moved to a niche role because of toxicity and interactions.

**Montelukast counseling.** Explain the neuropsychiatric warning. Ask about sleep, nightmares, mood and behavior at follow-up, especially in children and teens. Stop it if new symptoms appear. Many guidelines advise against using it for allergic rhinitis alone because the risk outweighs modest benefit.

**Theophylline safety.**
- Check levels when starting, after any interacting drug change, during febrile illness and when symptoms suggest toxicity.
- Toxicity can occur with levels that seem modest in chronic toxicity, especially in older adults; seizures and arrhythmias may occur without warning signs like nausea.
- Watch for drug additions: ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, fluvoxamine, cimetidine, allopurinol at higher exposures.
- Stopping smoking raises theophylline levels over days to weeks.
- Severe toxicity is treated with multiple-dose activated charcoal and hemodialysis; seizures are managed with benzodiazepines and barbiturates.

**Neurology overlap.**
- Theophylline lowers the seizure threshold; avoid in people with epilepsy where possible.
- Aminophylline has been used to reverse adenosine-mediated bradycardia after spinal cord injury and to treat apnea of prematurity (caffeine is preferred there).
- Zileuton requires liver monitoring and interacts with theophylline and warfarin.

**COPD.** Roflumilast reduces exacerbations in chronic bronchitis phenotype; monitor weight and mood, and avoid in people with depression or suicidal thoughts.

keyPoints: Cysteinyl leukotrienes act on CysLT1: bronchoconstriction, mucus, eosinophils
Montelukast (CysLT1 antagonist) has a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects
Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase; needs liver monitoring
Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: COX-1 block shunts to leukotrienes
Theophylline: narrow therapeutic index, CYP1A2 interactions, seizures via adenosine antagonism
Roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) reduces exacerbations in chronic bronchitis COPD

lessons.title: Biologics for Asthma

levels.kid: Some people have very bad asthma, even when they use their inhalers perfectly. For them, scientists made special medicines called biologics. They are like smart keys made from proteins, built to fit one exact lock in the immune system. Each one blocks a single troublemaking signal, like cutting just one wire in a noisy alarm instead of turning off the whole house. Doctors do blood tests first to find out which signal is causing the trouble, then pick the matching key. These medicines are given as a shot every few weeks, and they can make bad asthma attacks happen much less often.
levels.hs:
**Biologics** are lab-made **monoclonal antibodies** that target one specific molecule in the immune pathway. They are used for **severe asthma** that stays uncontrolled despite high-level inhaler treatment and good technique.

Most severe asthma is **type 2 (T2-high)**, driven by eosinophils and allergy signals. Blood tests help choose a biologic: **blood eosinophils**, **IgE** and exhaled nitric oxide (**FeNO**).

**The main biologics:**
- **Omalizumab:** binds **IgE**, for allergic asthma.
- **Mepolizumab** and **reslizumab:** block **IL-5**, the eosinophil growth signal.
- **Benralizumab:** binds the IL-5 receptor on eosinophils and marks them for destruction, nearly wiping them out.
- **Dupilumab:** blocks the receptor shared by **IL-4 and IL-13**; also used for eczema and nasal polyps.
- **Tezepelumab:** blocks **TSLP**, a signal from the airway lining at the top of the pathway, so it can help even with low eosinophils.

**Benefits:** fewer severe attacks, less need for steroid tablets, better lung function.

**Side effects:** injection-site reactions, rare allergic reactions (anaphylaxis, especially with omalizumab), and dupilumab can cause eye inflammation (conjunctivitis).

They are given as injections every two to eight weeks, often at home after training.
levels.college:
**Patient selection.** Severe asthma is asthma requiring high-intensity ICS plus a second controller (or oral steroids) to stay controlled, or remaining uncontrolled despite this. Before biologics: confirm the diagnosis, check adherence and technique, manage comorbidities and exposures. Phenotype with blood eosinophils, FeNO, total and specific IgE (including perennial allergen sensitization).

**Anti-IgE.** Omalizumab binds the Cε3 domain of free IgE, preventing binding to FcεRI on mast cells and basophils; FcεRI expression then falls. Dosing is based on total IgE and body weight. It forms small immune complexes, so total IgE measured after treatment is not useful. Anaphylaxis is rare but can be delayed, so initial doses are supervised and patients may carry adrenaline.

**Anti-IL-5 pathway.**
- Mepolizumab (subcutaneous) and reslizumab (IV, weight-based) neutralize IL-5.
- Benralizumab binds IL-5Rα; its afucosylated Fc enhances binding to FcγRIIIa on NK cells, causing antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) and near-complete eosinophil depletion.
- Best predictors: blood eosinophils (higher counts predict more benefit) and frequent exacerbations. They also reduce oral steroid requirement; mepolizumab is approved for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) and hypereosinophilic syndrome.

**Anti-IL-4Rα.** Dupilumab blocks IL-4Rα, inhibiting both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling (type I and type II receptors). It lowers FeNO and IgE and helps comorbid eczema and nasal polyps. A transient rise in blood eosinophils is common (blocked tissue trafficking via VCAM-1 and eotaxin); rarely, eosinophilic complications occur. Conjunctivitis is the classic adverse effect.

**Anti-TSLP.** Tezepelumab blocks TSLP upstream of T2 and some non-T2 inflammation, reducing exacerbations across eosinophil levels and lowering eosinophils, FeNO and IgE together.

**Response assessment** after about four months: exacerbations, oral steroid use, symptoms, lung function. Switch if response is poor.
levels.phd:
**Why antibody engineering matters.** Benralizumab's afucosylation increases FcγRIIIa affinity many-fold, converting a receptor blocker into a depleting antibody, a design also used in oncology antibodies (obinutuzumab). Omalizumab binds only free IgE, not IgE already bound to FcεRI, so it does not cross-link receptors and trigger degranulation, a necessary design feature. Newer anti-IgE antibodies (ligelizumab) with higher affinity improved IgE suppression but did not beat omalizumab in chronic urticaria trials, showing that affinity is not everything.

**Eosinophil biology lessons.** Near-complete eosinophil depletion with benralizumab did not cause obvious harm in trials, challenging assumptions about eosinophil roles in host defense, though theoretical concerns remain for helminth infections. Anti-IL-5 therapy lowers blood eosinophils more than airway tissue eosinophils, and some patients with sputum eosinophilia despite treatment respond to switching to IL-5R depletion. Autoimmune airway responses (anti-IL-5 autoantibodies, eosinophil peroxidase antibodies) may explain persistent eosinophilia in some patients.

**EGPA unmasking.** Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis can be suppressed by oral corticosteroids. When biologics allow steroid tapering, latent vasculitis may emerge, presenting with neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), cardiomyopathy or rash; initial reports with leukotriene antagonists were attributed to the same steroid-withdrawal unmasking.

**Upstream versus downstream targeting.** Alarmin blockade (anti-TSLP, anti-IL-33 such as itepekimab and astegolimab, anti-ST2) acts on epithelial-driven inflammation affecting both T2 and non-T2 pathways. This is the most promising strategy for T2-low asthma, where options are few. Anti-IL-33 and anti-ST2 antibodies showed signals in COPD, especially in former smokers.

**Disease modification and remission.** A new treatment goal is clinical remission: no exacerbations, no oral steroids, stable lung function and minimal symptoms. Whether early biologic therapy changes the natural history, including airway remodeling (mucus plugs that regress on treatment), is an active research question. Dupilumab and mepolizumab are now also approved for COPD with eosinophilia.
levels.expert:
**Workflow in a severe asthma clinic.**
- Confirm asthma and severity; exclude mimics (inducible laryngeal obstruction, bronchiectasis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, EGPA).
- Address adherence (prescription refills, inhaler counters), technique, smoking and vaping, obesity, reflux, rhinosinusitis and anxiety.
- Phenotype: blood eosinophils (measured several times, ideally off oral steroids), FeNO, total IgE, specific IgE to perennial allergens, and stool testing or treatment for parasites in at-risk patients (helminth infection must be treated before eosinophil-targeting biologics).

**Choosing.**
- Allergic with appropriate IgE: omalizumab.
- High eosinophils with frequent exacerbations: anti-IL-5 or anti-IL-5R.
- High FeNO, comorbid eczema or nasal polyps: dupilumab (avoid when eosinophils are very high, given the risk of eosinophilic complications).
- Low T2 markers: tezepelumab.
- Oral steroid dependence: anti-IL-5/5R or dupilumab have the strongest steroid-sparing data.

**Safety and monitoring.**
- Supervise first doses; train patients to recognize anaphylaxis, particularly with omalizumab.
- Taper oral steroids gradually after response, watching for adrenal insufficiency and for EGPA unmasking (new neuropathy, rash, cardiac symptoms, rising eosinophils).
- Dupilumab conjunctivitis needs ophthalmology input when severe.
- Live vaccines are generally avoided with some biologics; review the schedule.

**Neuro link.** EGPA commonly presents with mononeuritis multiplex, such as foot drop or wrist drop, and can cause strokes. A severe asthmatic with a new painful foot drop and rising eosinophils needs urgent vasculitis assessment.

**Measuring success.** Reassess at about four months: halving exacerbations and cutting oral steroids are meaningful responses; non-responders switch to a different mechanism.

keyPoints: Biologics treat severe asthma uncontrolled despite optimized inhaled therapy
Omalizumab binds free IgE (allergic asthma); anaphylaxis is rare but possible
Mepolizumab/reslizumab block IL-5; benralizumab depletes eosinophils via ADCC
Dupilumab blocks IL-4Rα (IL-4 and IL-13); conjunctivitis and transient eosinophilia
Tezepelumab blocks TSLP and works even with low eosinophils
Steroid tapering on biologics can unmask EGPA (e.g., mononeuritis multiplex)
